accepted.question_text: Let Γ and ∆ be residually soluble groups and let ψ: Γ -> ∆ be a homomorphism such that the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(ψ): PS(Γ) -> PS(∆) is an isomorphism. Determine how far ψ can fail to be an isomorphism, and in particular what additional hypotheses on Γ and ∆, such as finite generation or finite presentation, force ψ itself to be an isomorphism.
accepted.context_brief: True prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck's problem

evidence.quote: Our main interest in this paper is the prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck’s problem. More precisely, let again Γ, ∆ be two groups and ψ : Γ −→ ∆ a homomorphism, but assume now that the groups are residually soluble. Assume that, at the true prosoluble level, the corresponding homomorphism PS(ψ) : PS(Γ) −→ PS(∆) is an isomorphism. How far from an isomorphism can ψ be? Additional requirements can be added on Γ and ∆ (such as finite generation, finite presentation, ...).

accepted.question_text: Let G be a complete Hausdorff topological group such that for every nontrivial element g in G there exists an open normal subgroup N not containing g with soluble quotient G/N. Find useful characterizations of when G is isomorphic to the true prosoluble completion PS(Γ) of a residually soluble group Γ, and decide in particular how to tell whether G is isomorphic to PS(Γ) for some finitely generated group Γ or for some finitely presented group Γ.

evidence.quote: Can one find interesting characterizations of those groups which are true prosoluble completions of residually soluble group? More precisely, let G be a complete Hausdorff topological group such that, for any g ∈ G, g 6= 1, there exists an open normal subgroup N of G not containing g such that G/N is soluble; how can it be decided whether G is isomorphic to PS(Γ) for some finitely generated group Γ? for some finitely presented group Γ?

accepted.question_text: Let Γ be the first Grigorchuk group, viewed inside its profinite completion PF(Γ). Determine whether there exists an element g in PF(Γ) but not in Γ such that the subgroup ∆ generated by Γ and g has the congruence subgroup property. Producing such an element would give a new example of a non-isomorphic inclusion ψ: Γ -> ∆ whose induced map on profinite completions PF(ψ) is an isomorphism.

evidence.quote: Open problem. Let Γ be the first Grigorchuk group; it is an infinite group which is residually a finite 2–group, and all its proper quotients are finite 2–groups.
The problem is to find an element g in the complement of Γ in PF(Γ) such that the subgroup ∆ of PF(Γ) generated by Γ and g has the congruence subgroup property.

This would provide one more example of a homomorphism ψ : Γ −→ ∆ which is not an isomorphism and which would be such that the homomorphism PF(ψ) is an isomorphism, namely one solution to the original Grothendieck problem of a different nature than the existing ones (from [PlaTa–86], [PlaTa–89], and [BriGr–04]).

accepted.question_text: For a group Γ that is not residually soluble, determine structural properties of the true prosoluble kernel Ker(Γ -> PS(Γ)) = intersection_{n>=0} D^n(Γ), where D^n(Γ) denotes the derived series terms. In particular, develop descriptions or invariants for this kernel in concrete families such as non-residually-soluble one-relator groups, wreath products of the type discussed in the paper, amalgamated free products of nilpotent groups over cyclic subgroups, parafree groups, and free-by-free groups that are not residually soluble.
accepted.context_brief: Structure of the true prosoluble kernel

evidence.quote: For groups which are not residually soluble, it is a natural problem to find out properties of the true prosoluble kernel.

Examples to investigate include: ◦ other one–relator groups which are not residually soluble; ◦ wreath products as in (6.B); ◦ free products of nilpotent groups with amalgamation (see for example Proposition 7 in [Kahro1]); ◦ parafree groups (see (7.B)); ◦ meta–residually soluble groups, namely groups having a residually soluble normal subgroup with residually soluble quotient (see Theorem 2 in [Kahro2]); particular cases: free–by–free groups which are not residually soluble.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether there exists a discrete group Γ that is both residually finite and residually soluble, so that the canonical maps Γ -> PF(Γ) and Γ -> PS(Γ) are injective, but for which the canonical map Γ -> PFS(Γ) to the prosoluble completion built from finite soluble quotients is not injective.
accepted.context_brief: Separating true and finite prosoluble kernels

evidence.quote: (6.G) Does there exist a discrete group Γ which on the one hand is residually finite and residually soluble, namely for which both homomorphisms Γ −→ PF(Γ), Γ −→ PS(Γ) are injective, and which on the other hand is such that the homomorphism Γ −→ PFS(Γ) is NOT injective?

accepted.question_text: Determine whether there exist a finitely generated free group F, a group Γ that is residually soluble but not free, and a homomorphism ψ: F -> Γ such that for every j >= 1 the induced map F/D^j(F) -> Γ/D^j(Γ) is an isomorphism, equivalently such that the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(ψ): PS(F) -> PS(Γ) is an isomorphism.
accepted.context_brief: Free versus nonfree groups with identical prosoluble completion

evidence.quote: We do not know if there exist a finitely generated free group F, a group Γ which is residually soluble and not free, and a homomorphism ψ : F −→ Γ such that ψ induces an isomorphism F/Dj(F) −→ Γ/Dj(Γ) for all j ≥ 1, or equivalently such that PS(ψ) : PS(F) −→ PS(Γ) is an isomorphism.

trace.notes: Section hierarchy: 1. Introduction; 2. Completion with respect to a directed set of normal subgroups; 3. Universal property; 4. Examples of directed sets of normal subgroups; 5. True prosoluble completions; 6. Examples; 7. On the true prosoluble and the true pronilpotent analogues of Grothendieck’s problem; References. Definitions and notation introduced early include the profinite completion PF(Γ), the true prosoluble completion PS(Γ), the true pronilpotent completion PNi(Γ), the canonical maps ϕF and ϕS, derived series notation Dn(G), and kernels of canonical completion maps. The main theorem-like reference clusters appear in Sections 2 through 5 and in the lemma/consequence on pages 11-12. Likely open-problem regions are the introduction on page 2, Section 4.H on pages 7-8, Section 6.F-6.G on page 11, and Section 7.C on page 13.

The introduction contains two explicit open questions: the true prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck's problem and the characterization problem for topological groups that arise as true prosoluble completions. It also points ahead to later open-problem sections.
Sections 2 and 3 develop completion machinery and universal properties but do not introduce distinct open problems.
Section 4 yields one explicit open problem in subsection 4.H concerning the Grigorchuk group and the congruence subgroup property.
Section 5 is structural background on true prosoluble completions and derived series quotients; it does not add new open questions.
Section 6 contains one broad investigation problem about the true prosoluble kernel for non-residually-soluble groups and one explicit existence question about injectivity into PFS(Γ).
Section 7 contains one unresolved existence problem in subsection 7.C; subsection 7.B describes related pronilpotent results and examples but no distinct new open question beyond motivating context.

Expanded the paper's compressed statement into a standalone formulation by naming the induced completion map PS(ψ) and making the finite-generation and finite-presentation constraints explicit as hypotheses one may impose.
Made the ambient topological-group condition self-contained by inlining the separation property quantified over nontrivial elements and open normal subgroups with soluble quotients.
Rewrote the Grigorchuk-group open problem as a self-contained existence question and retained the stated consequence that solving it would yield a new Grothendieck-type example.

Converted the programmatic request to study Ker(Γ -> PS(Γ)) into a standalone problem by spelling out the kernel as the intersection of derived-series terms and listing the example families explicitly named by the paper.
Restated the existence problem in self-contained form by distinguishing the injective maps into PF(Γ) and PS(Γ) from the noninjective map into PFS(Γ).
Inlined the equivalence between isomorphisms on all derived-series quotients and an isomorphism on true prosoluble completions, keeping the free-versus-nonfree contrast explicit.

No candidates were merged. The introduction's broad Grothendieck-type problem, the Grigorchuk specialization, and the free-versus-nonfree Section 7 problem are related but mathematically distinct because they impose different hypotheses and target different constructions.

All accepted items passed self-containedness, evidence coverage, evidence completeness, no-new-facts, and schema conformance checks. Each accepted question has at least one complete-sentence verbatim quote with a page number, and no item relies on unresolved section or theorem references for comprehension.
